name: crewAI

facts.description: Framework for orchestrating role-playing, autonomous AI agents. By fostering collaborative intelligence, CrewAI empowers agents to work together seamlessly, tackling complex tasks.

title: CrewAI: A Python Framework for Orchestrating Multi-Agent AI Workflows
answer: CrewAI is an open-source Python framework for orchestrating role-playing autonomous AI agents that collaborate on complex tasks. It sits in the orchestration layer of the AI stack, above language models and tools, letting developers define agents with roles, goals and backstories, assign them tasks, and run them as a crew. The one thing to know before adopting it is that its production story rests on Flows, a thin deterministic backbone, not on unbounded agent autonomy.

sections.body: CrewAI is made by CrewAI Inc, the company behind the crewAIInc/crewAI repository, and is released under the MIT licence. It is a Python framework for orchestrating role-playing, autonomous AI agents, and its own description frames it as fostering collaborative intelligence so agents work together on complex tasks. The repository has been active recently, with a last push in October 2026, and the official site is crewai.com. In the AI stack it occupies the orchestration layer: it does not train models or serve them, it coordinates agents that are themselves powered by language models, giving them roles, goals, backstories, tools and tasks. The site describes it as an open-source framework for building and orchestrating multi-agent AI workflows, and it is powered by LLMs rather than being one.
sections.heading: What it is and where it sits in AI work

sections.body: The concrete jobs CrewAI handles are multi-step, language-heavy automations where several specialists collaborate. The site's examples include a researcher agent that uncovers emerging technologies, a task that produces a three-paragraph report, and a crew that runs those tasks sequentially. Agents can use external tools such as web search through SerperDevTool, and the framework supports conditional branching, state management and custom business logic through Flows. The site positions it for tasks requiring reasoning, unstructured data, API and tool calls, and collaborating agents in research, analysis, drafting and review. It is strongest where a team wants role-based crews with shared memory and handoffs, and where the work is cognitive rather than deterministic UI automation, which the site contrasts with enterprise RPA platforms.
sections.heading: What it is used for and where it is strongest

sections.body: CrewAI is a Python framework, so fluency in Python is the first prerequisite. The site's tutorial shows the core vocabulary a beginner must absorb: agents with role, goal and backstory, tasks with description and expected output, a crew that collects agents and tasks, a process such as Process.sequential, and kickoff() to start execution. No mathematics beyond ordinary programming is implied by the material, and no systems knowledge is required to run the examples, though production use brings in tracing, guardrails and cost control. The official site offers a developer portal, an MCP server and an llms-full.txt file aimed at agent-ready documentation, plus tutorials that walk through installing crewai and crewai-tools and storing API keys in environment variables. The learning curve is therefore moderate for a Python developer and steeper for someone new to LLM application patterns.
sections.heading: How hard it is to learn and what you need first

sections.body: The ecosystem around CrewAI is visible in the site's own pages. There is a crewai-tools package for external tools, an integration with Cerebras inference that lets agents run Llama 3.1 models through the Cerebras API, and a collaboration with NVIDIA that fully integrates CrewAI with NVIDIA NIM microservices as part of NVIDIA AI Enterprise. The site also lists an Agent Management Platform, tracing, guardrails, a developer portal, an MCP server and llms-full.txt. Community scale is suggested by the repository's roughly 59,000 stars and by a page citing 40,000 GitHub stars alongside 60 percent of the Fortune 500 and 1.4 billion agentic automations. The site publishes survey reports and blog guidance, and it links to a GitHub repository and an NVIDIA blueprint for technical demos.
sections.heading: Ecosystem and community

sections.body: CrewAI is presented as serving both ends. The tutorial shows a short script that defines agents, tasks and a crew and runs it with kickoff(), which is a fast path to a working prototype. For production, the site argues that the gap in agentic AI is architecture rather than intelligence, and it describes Agentic Systems built from Flows, a deterministic backbone, plus intelligence deployed where it matters. Flows are described as a very thin code layer with almost no abstractions, using decorators and state management, handling conditional branching and custom business logic with the same inputs producing the same execution path. The cost of this dual nature is that teams must learn both the loose crew model and the tighter Flow model, and the site warns against unbounded agency and against prompt chains passing as agents.
sections.heading: Prototyping speed against production performance

sections.body: The site's own claims point to substantial enterprise adoption. One page states 60 percent of the Fortune 500, 1.4 billion agentic automations and 40,000 GitHub stars, and cites production use cases at PwC and the startup Parloa. A survey report based on 500 C-level executives and senior leaders at organizations with over 100 million dollars in revenue says 81 percent have fully adopted or are actively scaling agentic AI, 65 percent already use AI agents, and 57 percent prefer building on existing open-source tools rather than starting from scratch. The site also reports that security and governance top evaluation factors at 34 percent, and that data readiness and insufficient talent are the leading obstacles. These figures come from CrewAI's own material, so they should be read as vendor-published rather than independent, but they indicate that CrewAI is a current choice rather than a legacy one for Python-first agent work.
sections.heading: Industry adoption and careers

sections.body: CrewAI is Python-first, and the site contrasts it with Microsoft Agent Framework, which targets .NET and Azure ecosystems, and with Automation Anywhere, an enterprise RPA platform for UI and legacy system automation. The site's comparison page also lists AutoGen and MetaGPT among multi-agent frameworks buyers consider. The polyglot pattern it belongs to is one where CrewAI handles LLM-driven reasoning, tool use and dynamic task decomposition, while RPA tools handle deterministic UI workflows, and the site says many enterprises use both. It integrates with model providers such as Cerebras and with NVIDIA NIM microservices, so it typically sits alongside an inference provider, a tool layer and an observability or management layer rather than replacing them.
sections.heading: How it fits beside the others

sections.body: The site itself names weaknesses. It criticizes implementations that are too rigid or too loose, warns that prompt chains are not agents, and argues that DAGs and graphs can hurt maintainability. It notes that extended reasoning can consume tens of thousands of tokens before a short answer, that a ten-step agent run can reach hundreds of thousands to two million tokens, and that a large share of enterprise token spend goes to use cases without proven business value. The material does not give independent benchmarks, does not detail pricing for the Agent Management Platform, and does not settle how well Flows perform outside the vendor's own reported cases. Questions about long-term maintenance, model portability and governance specifics remain open in what the official pages say.
sections.heading: Limits and open questions
